title: The Night the Sky Fell
sum: Enoch begins a new set of teachings for his son Methuselah: two dreams he saw before he married. In the first, seen as a boy in his grandfather Mahalalel's house, the sky crashes onto the earth and the earth sinks into a great abyss. He cries out in his sleep. Mahalalel tells him the dream is about the sin of the whole earth, which is about to be destroyed, and urges him to pray that a remnant will be left.

Enoch goes outside at dawn and sees the sun rise, the moon set and the stars in their places. The order of the sky reassures him, and he blesses "the Lord of judgment." The dream is the Flood, seen long before it comes.
readings: Read as a call to prayer
The dream is not just a warning but a summons. A boy who sees the end of the world is told to pray, and the next chapter shows that his prayer is heard: a remnant, Noah's family, survives.

The Flood dream is the first of a pair. The second (chapters 85–90) ends with the last judgment. Enoch remembers the first dream when he wakes from the second (90:42). The Flood is the pattern for the end.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches count 1 Enoch as Scripture, so the chapter is received as a true vision given to Enoch (Cowley; Asale): God warns before he judges, and the prayers of the righteous are heard. It is read alongside the Flood story of Genesis 6–9.
views.H: Scholars see chapters 83–84 as a short introduction to the Animal Apocalypse, perhaps written separately, set in Enoch's youth to give the dreams authority. Its Flood theme links the judgment of the Watchers' age with the judgment the writers expected in their own day.
views.N: The pairing of Flood and final judgment is the same one Jesus uses (Matthew 24:37–39) and 2 Peter 3:5–7 develops. The title "Lord of glory" appears in 1 Corinthians 2:8 and James 2:1.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition knows Enoch little, and often less kindly, but the theme of a righteous man praying for his generation before the Flood is close to later Jewish stories about Noah warning his neighbors.
views.W: Most churches find here an ancient Jewish witness to prayer for the world and to the Flood as a type of judgment, and test it against Genesis, which names no such prayer.

deep.b: Enoch dates both dreams by his marriage: the first "when I was learning to write," the second before he married Edna (83:2; 85:3). In Genesis Enoch's son Methuselah is born when Enoch is 65 (Genesis 5:21). So the dreams come at the very start of his life. The point is that the seer saw the whole course of history before any of it happened, even before his own family began.

echoes: Genesis 5:12–24; Genesis 6:5–8; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 8:22; Matthew 24:37–39; 2 Peter 3:5–7

settings.when: after the teaching on the stars (72–82), as Enoch hands on his books
settings.why: To give Methuselah the two dreams so he can pass them on. The frame makes every later reader one more link in the chain from father to son.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 160s BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV and the revolt led by Judas Maccabeus. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

settings.what: The first dream: the sky falls
settings.to: Methuselah; inside the story, the boy Enoch alone, asleep in Mahalalel's house
settings.when: when Enoch was a boy learning to write
settings.why: To show the coming Flood as creation coming undone, so that its hearers feel how total God's judgment on sin is.
settings.readers: For readers in the 160s BC, who believed a second judgment was near, the first judgment was a pattern: the God who ended the old world could end their oppressors' world too.

settings.to: the boy Enoch, woken from his nightmare
settings.why: To tell him what the dream means (the earth will be destroyed for its sin) and what to do about it (pray for a remnant). The old man turns fear into prayer.
settings.readers: Readers facing their own crisis learned the same lesson: a vision of judgment calls for prayer, not despair.

title: Enoch's Prayer for the Earth
sum: Enoch lifts his hands and prays. He praises God as King of kings, maker and ruler of all, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, who knows and sees everything. Then he names the problem: the angels of heaven are doing wrong, and God's anger rests on humanity until the great day of judgment.
He asks God not to wipe out all flesh and leave the earth empty, but to destroy only the flesh that has angered him, and to plant the righteous as a seed that lasts forever.

views.E: For readers in the Ethiopian Orthodox churches, which count the book as Scripture, the prayer is a prayer of the patriarch Enoch, and its request is answered in Noah. Its praise stays close to the Psalms.
views.H: Scholars note how much the prayer sounds like other Jewish prayers of the Second Temple period, built from the Psalms and Isaiah. It assumes the Watchers story (6–16) as the reason for the Flood, so it was written by someone who knew that story.
views.N: The prayer shares language with the New Testament: "King of kings" (1 Timothy 6:15; Revelation 19:16), heaven as throne and earth as footstool (Matthew 5:34–35; Acts 7:49), nothing impossible for God (Luke 1:37).
views.J: The structure of praise, confession of the problem, and request follows Jewish prayer as later fixed in the synagogue, and many of its phrases have parallels in Jewish prayers.
views.W: Most churches can read this prayer with little to object to; it stays close to the Psalms. The question is not its theology but its claim to be Enoch's own words.

deep.b: Almost every line of the prayer has a parallel in the Hebrew Bible: God's kingship over all generations (Psalm 145:13), heaven as throne and earth as footstool (Isaiah 66:1), nothing too hard for God (Jeremiah 32:17), God who sees everything (Psalm 139:1–12), Israel as God's planting (Isaiah 60:21). The prayer shows how a Jewish writer of the 200s or 100s BC prayed in the words of Scripture.

echoes: Psalm 145:13; Isaiah 66:1; Jeremiah 32:17; Psalm 139:1–12; Isaiah 60:21; 1 Timothy 6:15; Matthew 5:34–35

settings.when: the morning after his dream of the earth's destruction
settings.why: To praise God and ask him to spare a remnant of humanity from the coming Flood. The prayer shows that God listens and that the righteous have a part in the world's survival.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 160s BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV and the revolt led by Judas Maccabeus. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

title: A White Bull from the Earth
sum: Enoch tells Methuselah his second dream. A white bull comes out of the earth, then a young cow, and two calves, one black and one red. The black calf gores the red one and chases it away for good. The cow searches and wails until the white bull comforts her. She bears another white bull, and many cattle and black calves.

This is the beginning of the Animal Apocalypse: Adam, Eve, Cain and Abel, Seth, and the line of Genesis 5, all as cattle. Nobody is named. The reader has to recognize the story of Genesis in its animal disguise.
readings: Each animal stands for a person or people, and the colors judge them: white is righteous, black is sinful, red is blood. The reader decodes it with Genesis open.
Like Nathan's parable to David (2 Samuel 12:1–7) or Jotham's fable of the trees (Judges 9:7–15), the animal story lets the reader see familiar events at a distance, and see them freshly.

views.E: In the Ethiopian Orthodox churches, which receive 1 Enoch as Scripture, the dream is read as prophecy shown to Enoch before it happened, and in the church's Christian reading of the book (Asale) its end is read with Christ in view. How each animal is read in the church's own commentary tradition has not been checked for this page.
views.H: Scholars call chapters 85–90 the Animal Apocalypse and date it to the Maccabean crisis, about 164–160 BC. Its retelling of Genesis follows the Hebrew Bible closely but chooses what to show: violence, lines of descent, and the white line of the righteous.
views.N: The Animal Apocalypse is one of the clearest pre-Christian examples of a sweeping review of history leading to judgment, like the speech of Stephen in Acts 7 or the history of faith in Hebrews 11.
views.J: Jewish tradition knew the habit of picturing people as animals from the Bible, and the Animal Apocalypse is an early, full example. Copies of it were kept at Qumran.
views.W: Most churches read the vision as a remarkable Jewish interpretation of the Bible's story from before Christ, useful for seeing how Jews then read Genesis, but not as inspired prophecy.

Identifications follow the commentaries of Tiller and Nickelsburg; where they agree, there is little debate.

The writer had good models: the Bible calls Israel a flock and its enemies beasts, and Daniel 7–8 has empires as beasts and kings as a ram and a goat. But the Animal Apocalypse goes further. Its animals follow the food laws: Israel is a clean animal, sheep; the nations are unclean predators and scavengers (Leviticus 11). David Bryan argues that the whole vision is built on this "kosher" map of the world. The picture also lets the writer show change: the righteous line moves from cattle to sheep, and at the end everyone becomes cattle again.

The Animal Apocalypse survives complete only in Ge'ez. Pieces of it are in four Aramaic copies from Qumran Cave 4 (4Q204, 4Q205, 4Q206, 4Q207), the oldest of which, 4Q207, Milik dated to about 150–125 BC, and a short Greek passage of 89:42–49 survives in a Vatican manuscript. The variants on these pages compare Dillmann's text, the EOTC printed text, the Vatican Greek and Charles; the evidence of the two Ethiopic manuscript families and the readings of the Aramaic fragments have not been weighed here.

echoes: Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:21–22; Genesis 4:1–25; Genesis 5:1–32; Jubilees 4:1–12; Hebrews 11:4

settings.what: The second dream vision: the Animal Apocalypse
settings.to: his son Methuselah, and through him "the generations" to come
settings.when: a dream Enoch saw before he married, told in his old age
settings.why: To show that the whole of history, from Adam to the end, is known and ruled by God, that the wrongs Israel suffers are recorded, and that God will judge the angels and nations who abused his flock and make a new start for all.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 160s BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV and the revolt led by Judas Maccabeus. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).
views: Most scholars: 164–160 BC, because the vision knows Judas Maccabeus's battles but not his death. A few older scholars dated it later, to John Hyrcanus (134–104 BC).
Many link it to the "lambs" of 90:6, a reform group that saw itself as the faithful remnant; some to the Hasideans of 1 Maccabees 2:42.

title: Stars Among the Cattle
sum: A single star falls from the sky and grazes among the cattle. Then many stars come down and join it, living among the calves and cattle. They mount the cows, and father elephants, camels and donkeys. The cattle are terrified. The new beasts bite and gore and then begin to eat the cattle, and all the children of the earth tremble and run.
This is the story of the Watchers (chapters 6–11) in animal form: fallen angels as stars, their giant children as huge beasts, and the violence that filled the earth before the Flood.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches read 1 Enoch's text, in which the Watchers are angels. But Bruk Ayele Asale reports that the church's traditional commentary (andəmta) often explains the Watchers as children of Seth who came down from the holy mountain, as in the Ethiopic Conflict of Adam and Eve. Both readings are found in the church.
views.H: Scholars note that the vision combines the two strands of the Watchers story, Asael's teaching and Shemihazah's marriages, putting Asael first. That suggests the writer knew the Book of the Watchers in something like its present form.
views.N: Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels who left their place and were kept in chains, and 1 Peter 3:19–20 links imprisoned spirits with Noah's day. Revelation's falling star (Revelation 9:1) and the dragon sweeping stars from the sky (Revelation 12:4) use the same picture of stars as angels.
views.J: Rabbinic Judaism mostly turned away from the angel reading of Genesis 6:1–4: Genesis Rabbah 26:5 says "the sons of God" were sons of judges or nobles. The Qumran community kept the angel reading, as 1 Enoch does.
views.W: Many church fathers read Genesis 6 as Enoch does, but from the 300s on most (Augustine, City of God 15.23) read "sons of God" as the line of Seth, and many churches still do. Readers today are divided.

deep.h: Two lines in Genesis 6, two readings
deep.b: Genesis 6:2 says "the sons of God" took human wives. 1 Enoch reads them as angels, the Watchers, and so do Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 by most readings. From the 300s on, many Christians (Augustine, Chrysostom) and the rabbis read them as human beings: the godly line of Seth, or rulers. The Animal Apocalypse is one of the earliest, clearest pictures of the angel reading: the "sons of God" are stars that fall.

echoes: Genesis 6:1–4; Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4; 1 Peter 3:19–20; Revelation 9:1; Revelation 12:4; Daniel 8:10

title: Seven Men in White
sum: As the beasts gore and eat each other and the earth cries out, Enoch looks up and sees beings like white men come from heaven: four, and three more with them. The three take Enoch by the hand, lift him away from the earth, and set him on a high place where he can see a tower towering over all the hills. They tell him to stay and watch what will happen to the elephants, camels, donkeys, stars and cattle.
In the code, men are angels. Enoch, who has not appeared in his own dream, enters it now: he is taken up, as Genesis says God took him, to watch the rest of history from God's side.

views.E: For readers who receive the book as Scripture, as the Ethiopian Orthodox churches do, this explains Enoch's taking up (Genesis 5:24): he was lifted to God's presence and, with Elijah, returns before the end (90:31).
views.H: Scholars read the scene as the vision's way of placing Enoch as an observer above history. The seven archangels are those of 20:1–8; their number is part of Jewish belief by the 200s BC (Tobit 12:15).
views.N: Hebrews 11:5 says Enoch was taken so that he did not see death. Revelation's seven angels who stand before God (Revelation 8:2) are the same group.
views.J: Later Jewish mysticism made Enoch, taken to heaven, into the angel Metatron (3 Enoch). The Animal Apocalypse already places him in heaven as a witness, though not as an angel.
views.W: Most churches read the scene as a Jewish expansion of Genesis 5:24, interesting for the history of belief about angels, but not as a revealed account of where Enoch went.

echoes: Genesis 5:24; Hebrews 11:5; Daniel 8:15; Daniel 10:5; Tobit 12:15; Revelation 8:2

settings.when: after they lift him from the earth
settings.why: To make Enoch a witness of everything that follows. What he sees, he will tell; the reader receives the history as an eyewitness report from heaven.
settings.readers: Most scholars: a Jewish scribal group in Judea in the 160s BC, during the persecution under Antiochus IV and the revolt led by Judas Maccabeus. Ethiopian Orthodox readers receive it as Enoch's own words, kept for the last generations (1:2).

title: The Stars Bound
sum: One of the first four angels seizes the first fallen star, ties its hands and feet, and throws it into a narrow, deep, dark abyss. Another draws a sword and gives it to the elephants, camels and donkeys, and they strike each other until the earth shakes. A third throws stones from heaven, gathers all the stars that had acted like horses, ties them, and throws them into a crack in the earth.
This is the judgment of chapter 10 in short: Raphael binds Asael, Gabriel sets the giants against each other, and Michael binds Shemihazah's company.

views.E: Readers in the Ethiopian Orthodox churches, which count both 1 Enoch and Jude as Scripture, can read the binding as the background of Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 (Asale studies how the church reads Enoch with Jude). How the andəmta commentary explains the Watchers is noted on chapter 86.
views.H: Scholars note that the chapter follows chapter 10 closely, which shows the Animal Apocalypse was written by someone who knew the Book of the Watchers.
views.N: Jude 6 says God keeps rebel angels "in everlasting chains down in the gloom," and Revelation 20:1–3 has an angel bind Satan and throw him into the abyss. The pattern of binding before final judgment is the same.
views.J: The binding of angels in the earth also appears in Jubilees 5:6–10. Rabbinic texts mostly do not take it up.
views.W: Most churches agree that some angels sinned and are kept for judgment (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4), without accepting the details of 1 Enoch's account.

title: From the Ark to the Ruined House
sum: The longest chapter of 1 Enoch runs from Noah to the return from exile. An angel teaches the white bull, Noah, who becomes a man and builds a boat; the Flood drowns the giants. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob follow as a white bull, a white bull and a white sheep. From Jacob on, Israel are sheep. Wolves (Egypt) oppress them; the Lord of the sheep leads them through the split sea, shows himself at the rock, and Moses' sheep builds him a house. The sheep go blind and see again through the judges and kings. Rams (Saul, David, Solomon) lead them, and a tower, the Temple, rises on the house.

Then the sheep wander again and kill the sheep sent to them. The Lord abandons his house to lions and leopards and hands the flock to seventy shepherds, angels who are to punish them within limits, while another angel writes down every excess. The shepherds go far beyond their orders. The tower burns and the house is torn down. Three sheep return and rebuild it, but the bread on its table is defiled.
readings: The chapter follows the Bible's history in order, from Genesis to Ezra and Nehemiah. Each event the Bible tells is there, often in a single line, and some (the giving of the Law, the covenant with David) are strikingly absent.
Read as an answer to suffering

Why has God's people suffered so long under foreign powers? The vision answers: God handed them over for their sins, but the angels he set over them went too far, and every excess is written down. The suffering is not forgotten, and it will be judged.

views.E: Readers in the Ethiopian Orthodox churches, which count the book as Scripture, receive the chapter as a prophecy of Israel's history shown to Enoch before it happened. Elijah's being taken up to Enoch (89:52) fits the church's expectation that the two will return together (see chapter 90).
views.H: Scholars read the chapter as history told as prophecy, up to the writer's own time. Its choices show the writer's views: no mention of the Law at Sinai, a negative view of the Second Temple from its first day (89:73), and a theory of angelic shepherds to explain why Israel has been ruled by nations since the exile.
views.N: Many New Testament themes appear here: Israel killing its prophets (Matthew 23:37), God leaving his house (Matthew 23:38), the bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 behind the Good Shepherd of John 10, and the angelic powers over the nations (Ephesians 6:12). The Epistle of Barnabas 16:5 quotes this chapter's picture of the sheep, their fold and their tower handed over to destruction.
views.J: The idea of seventy angels over seventy nations is found in later Jewish texts (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Deuteronomy 32:8). The rabbis also count seventy nations. The rejection of the Second Temple fits groups like those behind the Dead Sea Scrolls, not the mainstream that later became rabbinic Judaism.
views.W: Most churches value the chapter as an early Jewish reading of Israel's history, especially its witness to belief in angels over the nations (Daniel 10:13, 20). They test its claims, such as the impure Second Temple, against Haggai, Zechariah and Ezra, who saw that Temple as God's will.

The vision never mentions the Law given at Sinai, the covenant with Abraham or with David, or the Davidic promise of an everlasting kingdom. It treats the Second Temple as impure from the start. Some scholars think these silences show a group whose authority came from Enoch's revelation and whose hopes did not center on the Temple or the line of David. Others warn against reading too much into the silences of an animal fable.

deep.title: Builders who become men
deep.b: My suggestion, offered as speculation: in this vision only two animals "become men," Noah (89:1) and Moses (89:36), and each, right after, builds what God asks for, a boat and a house. The tower built in Solomon's day (89:50), and the tower rebuilt after the exile (89:73), are built without anyone becoming a man. At the end it is God himself who brings the new house (90:29). The change into a "man" may mark a builder working by heavenly instruction, like Moses building by the pattern shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:9, 40). On that reading, the vision's verdict on the Temples is that no one built them by heavenly pattern, so only God can build the true one. Others have noted the link between becoming a man and building; I do not know of anyone who has drawn this conclusion from it.

echoes: Genesis 6–9; Genesis 12–50; Exodus 1–40; Numbers 20:28; Deuteronomy 34:5–8; Judges 2:11–19; 1 Samuel 13–31; 1 Kings 6–8; 2 Kings 2:11; 2 Kings 25:8–10; Ezra 1–6; Ezekiel 34; Zechariah 1:12–15; Zechariah 11:4–17; Matthew 23:37–38

settings.what: The commission of the seventy shepherds
settings.to: seventy shepherds (angels) and their companions; then another angel who is to keep the record
settings.when: after God abandons his house and tower to the nations
settings.why: To hand Israel over for punishment within set limits, and to make sure every excess is written down. Inside the story, the shepherds hear only their orders; the recording angel hears that they will go too far.
settings.readers: For Jews under Seleucid persecution, the speech answered the question why God let the nations rule Israel so long: God set limits, the powers broke them, and the record will be opened (90:17, 20).
views: Most scholars: the shepherds are angels set over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8; Daniel 10:13, 20).
Some older scholars: they are Gentile kings who ruled Israel.

settings.what: The Lord's charge to the sheep, and the warning to the wolves
settings.by: the Lord of the sheep; then Moses and Aaron
settings.to: Moses (the sheep who escaped); then the meeting of the wolves, Pharaoh's court
settings.when: after the Lord comes down at the sheep's cry
settings.why: To warn the oppressors before judgment falls. The wolves are told plainly not to touch the sheep, so their later punishment is just.
settings.readers: Readers under Antiochus IV could hear in it the hope that God warns tyrants first and then acts, as he did with Pharaoh.

settings.what: The sheep's cry at the rock
settings.to: the sheep with them (Aaron) and their leader (Moses)
settings.when: at Sinai, when the Lord appears
settings.why: To express Israel's terror before God's presence and ask for a go-between, as in Exodus 20:18–19.
settings.readers: For a group that looked to Enoch as its own go-between with heaven, the scene showed that God's people had always needed someone to stand between them and God.

settings.when: as the sheep are thrown to the wild animals
settings.why: To plead for Israel. Enoch does not stand above the story; he grieves and intercedes.
settings.readers: For Jews suffering under the Seleucids, Enoch's cry was their own: it told them that their complaint had been raised in heaven long before, and was written down.

title: The Great Horn and the New House
sum: The shepherds hand the flock on until birds of prey come: eagles, vultures, kites and ravens, the Greek empires. They strip the sheep to the bone. Then lambs are born whose eyes are open. The ravens kill one of them, but horns grow on the lambs, and one great horn sprouts. Rams rally to it. The ravens and all the birds fight it but cannot break it, and the angel who keeps the record comes down to help. Here the vision reaches the writer's own day: Judas Maccabeus and the revolt against Antiochus IV.

Then God acts. The Lord of the sheep strikes the earth and it swallows the enemies. The sheep receive a great sword. A throne is set up in the land; the books are opened; the fallen stars and the seventy shepherds are thrown into a fiery abyss, and the blinded sheep into a fiery valley. God folds up the old house and brings a new, larger one, with no tower. The nations bow and join the sheep, the sword is sealed away, everyone can see, and a white bull is born. All become white cattle. Enoch wakes and weeps.
readings: Up to about 90:13–16 the vision tracks real events of the 160s BC. After that, it describes what the writer hoped God would soon do. Most scholars date the vision from that seam.
Read as prophecy of Christ and the church
Ethiopian and some other Christian readers read the white bull as Christ, the new house as the church or the heavenly Jerusalem, and the change of all into white cattle as the new creation.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches count the chapter as Scripture and read it in a Christian way (Asale). Christian readers of this kind take the white bull as Christ and the "word" of 90:38 as the Word made flesh (John 1:14). Ethiopian tradition expects Enoch and Elijah to return before Christ's coming (see the card below).
views.H: Most scholars date the vision to about 164–160 BC: it knows Judas Maccabeus's battles (90:9–16) but not his death in 160 BC. The doubled battle scenes (90:13–15 and 90:16–18) may show the writer updating his work. The white bull is a messianic figure who appears only after God has won.
views.N: The chapter's judgment scene (throne, books, fiery abyss) is close to Daniel 7, Matthew 25:31–46 and Revelation 20:11–15, and its new Jerusalem without a temple matches Revelation 21:22. The return of Enoch and Elijah was read by early Christians into the two witnesses of Revelation 11.
views.J: The vision's support for the Maccabees links it to the events Jews remember at Hanukkah. Its hopes, a new Jerusalem built by God and the conversion of the nations, fit Isaiah and the prophets. Later rabbinic Judaism did not keep 1 Enoch.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as a powerful pre-Christian Jewish hope, often strikingly close to the New Testament, but written by Jews of the 160s BC, not by Enoch, and not as Scripture.

Main sources: Charles (1912), Tiller (1993), Nickelsburg (2001), Olson (2013).

The vision follows history closely through the Greek period, then names a series of events that fit the 170s–160s BC: a lamb killed (perhaps Onias III, about 171 BC), horns on the lambs, a great horn (Judas Maccabeus, from 166 BC), a hard battle in which heaven helps (Beth-zur, 164 BC). Then it turns to God's direct intervention, which did not happen as described. It does not know that Judas died in battle in 160 BC (1 Maccabees 9:18). So most scholars date it between 164 and 160 BC. This makes it roughly the same age as Daniel 7–12. The oldest Aramaic copy of the Dream Visions (4Q207) is dated by Milik to about 150–125 BC, which fits. Nineteenth-century scholars who took the great horn as John Hyrcanus dated the vision some forty years later; the Qumran copies have made that view rare.

Daniel 7–8, written in the same crisis, also uses animals: four beasts from the sea, a ram and a goat, and a little horn that is Antiochus IV. The two visions share a horn for a ruler, books opened at a heavenly court, and a final kingdom for God's people. But they differ: Daniel's horn is the enemy king; Enoch's great horn is the Jewish hero. Daniel waits for God; Enoch arms the sheep.

The judgment of 90:20–27 follows a strict order: first the fallen stars (90:24), then the seventy shepherds (90:25), then the blinded sheep (90:26). Angels are judged before humans, and Israel's own apostates are judged alongside the powers that oppressed it.

traditions.q: Will Enoch and Elijah come back before the end?
views: Yes. Enoch (Henok) and Elijah, who were taken up without dying, will return before Christ's second coming as the two witnesses of Revelation 11, die as martyrs, and rise. 1 Enoch 89:52 and 90:31 are read as part of this teaching.
Widely held in Orthodox tradition: Hippolytus and many fathers taught that Enoch and Elijah will return to oppose the Antichrist, and Orthodox hymns and icons often show them together.

Many fathers and medieval theologians held it (Tertullian wrote that Enoch and Elijah are kept to die later and destroy the Antichrist), but the Church has never defined it. Many Catholic scholars now read the two witnesses of Revelation 11 as a symbol of the church's witness.
The two witnesses are two literal future prophets in Jerusalem; many think they are Moses and Elijah (Revelation 11:6 matches their miracles), some Enoch and Elijah.
Most Reformed interpreters read the two witnesses as a picture of the witnessing church, not two returning men, and give 1 Enoch no weight on the question.
